2025.clinched: Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, 7 December 2025, final round (24 of 24)
2025.note: Norris clinched his first championship at the Abu Dhabi finale on 7 December 2025, where third place behind race winner Max Verstappen and teammate Oscar Piastri was exactly enough. It was the first time since the four-way shootout of 2010 that more than two drivers reached the last race still in contention, and the two-point verdict, 423 to 421, ended Verstappen's run of four straight titles. Norris took seven wins along the way and gave McLaren a drivers' champion for the first time since Lewis Hamilton in 2008.

2024.clinched: Las Vegas Grand Prix, 23 November 2024, two rounds to spare (round 22 of 24)
2024.note: Verstappen sealed his fourth consecutive title under the Las Vegas lights on 23 November 2024, finishing fifth, one place ahead of his only remaining rival Lando Norris, with Qatar and Abu Dhabi still to run. The decisive blow had come three weeks earlier at a rain-soaked Interlagos, where he won from 17th on the grid. He closed the year on 437 points to Norris's 374 with nine wins, even as Red Bull surrendered the constructors' championship to McLaren.

2023.clinched: Qatar Grand Prix sprint race, Lusail, Saturday 7 October 2023, with six grands prix still to run (round 17 of 22)
2023.note: Verstappen's third title arrived on a Saturday: second place in the sprint race at the Qatar Grand Prix on 7 October 2023 settled it with six grands prix still to run, making him the first driver to clinch a championship in a sprint. The season rewrote the record book, with 19 wins from 22 races, ten of them in a row between Miami and Monza, and a final margin of 290 points over teammate Sergio Pérez.

2022.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Suzuka, 9 October 2022, four rounds to spare (round 18 of 22)
2022.note: Verstappen retained the title by winning a rain-shortened Japanese Grand Prix at Suzuka on 9 October 2022, a race that ran only 29 of its 53 laps, and at first nobody was certain he was champion: the paddock expected reduced points until the FIA confirmed full points applied. Charles Leclerc's five-second penalty for cutting the final chicane dropped him to third and closed the arithmetic with four rounds to spare. Verstappen's 15 wins that year set a new single-season record, and he finished 146 points clear of Leclerc.

2021.clinched: Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, 12 December 2021, final round (22 of 22)
2021.note: The championship went to the last lap of the last race: at Abu Dhabi on 12 December 2021, a late safety car for Nicholas Latifi's crash let Verstappen pit for soft tyres and pass Lewis Hamilton at Turn 5 on the final lap. The two had arrived at the finale level on points after 21 rounds. Verstappen became the first Dutch world champion, 395.5 points to 387.5, in a decider whose safety-car handling stayed controversial long after the flag, while Mercedes still collected an eighth straight constructors' title.

2020.clinched: Turkish Grand Prix, Istanbul Park, 15 November 2020, three rounds to spare (round 14 of 17)
2020.note: Hamilton equalled Michael Schumacher's record of seven championships at the Turkish Grand Prix on 15 November 2020, winning from sixth on the grid on a treacherous wet Istanbul Park surface and taking the flag more than 30 seconds clear. He ran roughly 50 laps on a single set of intermediate tyres while his only remaining rival, teammate Valtteri Bottas, spun six times on the way to 14th. The title came with three races to spare in a season of 11 wins and 347 points.

2019.clinched: United States Grand Prix, Circuit of The Americas, 3 November 2019, two rounds to spare (round 19 of 21)
2019.note: Second place behind teammate Valtteri Bottas at the United States Grand Prix on 3 November 2019 made Hamilton a six-time champion with two rounds to spare; he had needed only eighth. A one-stop gamble nearly won him the race itself, and he held off Max Verstappen by under a second at the flag in Austin. The 413-point, 11-win season left only Schumacher's seven titles ahead of him.

2018.clinched: Mexican Grand Prix, Mexico City, 28 October 2018, two rounds to spare (round 19 of 21)
2018.note: Fourth place at the Mexican Grand Prix on 28 October 2018 was enough to make Hamilton a five-time champion, level with Juan Manuel Fangio, with two races to spare. Sebastian Vettel needed victory to stay alive and finished second to race winner Max Verstappen; his challenge had never recovered from Hockenheim in July, where he slid out of the lead in light rain while Hamilton won from 14th. The final accounting read 408 points to 320, with 11 wins for Hamilton.

2017.clinched: Mexican Grand Prix, Mexico City, 29 October 2017, two rounds to spare (round 18 of 20)
2017.note: Hamilton took his fourth title at the Mexican Grand Prix on 29 October 2017 in the strangest way of any of them: ninth place, after Vettel's front wing clipped his right-rear tyre on the opening lap and sent both contenders to the pits. Vettel recovered from 19th to fourth but needed second, so the crown was settled with Brazil and Abu Dhabi still to race. Hamilton finished the year 46 points clear, 363 to 317, with nine wins.

2016.clinched: Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, 27 November 2016, final round (21 of 21)
2016.note: Rosberg only had to survive the Abu Dhabi finale on 27 November 2016, and did, taking the second place he needed while race leader and teammate Hamilton deliberately slowed to back him into Vettel and Verstappen over the closing laps. The five-point margin, 385 to 380, settled an all-Mercedes title fight and made Nico and Keke Rosberg the second father-and-son champions after the Hills. Five days later Rosberg announced his retirement from the sport, still champion.

2015.clinched: United States Grand Prix, Circuit of The Americas, 25 October 2015, three rounds to spare (round 16 of 19)
2015.note: Hamilton clinched title number three by winning a wet-dry, safety-car-strewn United States Grand Prix in Austin on 25 October 2015, with three rounds to spare. The decisive moment came late, when Rosberg ran wide from the lead and Hamilton pounced for his tenth win of a season he closed out on 381 points to Rosberg's 322. It made him the first British driver to win back-to-back championships and matched his hero Ayrton Senna on three titles.

2014.clinched: Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, 23 November 2014, final round (19 of 19)
2014.note: The title was decided at Abu Dhabi on 23 November 2014, the only F1 race ever to award double points, and Hamilton removed the suspense by beating polesitter Rosberg off the line and winning outright. Rosberg's ERS failed on lap 25 and he limped home 14th, refusing the team's suggestion to retire the car. Hamilton's second title, six years after his first, came with 11 wins to Rosberg's five, 384 points to 317, and it gave Mercedes a first drivers' champion since Fangio in 1955.

2013.clinched: Indian Grand Prix, Buddh International Circuit, 27 October 2013, three rounds to spare (round 16 of 19)
2013.note: Vettel won the Indian Grand Prix on 27 October 2013 to take a fourth consecutive championship with three rounds to spare, then celebrated with doughnuts in front of the Buddh grandstands. He kept winning to the end: victories in Abu Dhabi, Austin and Brazil completed a run of nine straight wins to close the season, equalling Alberto Ascari's record streak. Thirteen wins and a 155-point margin over Fernando Alonso made it the most crushing of his four titles.

2012.clinched: Brazilian Grand Prix, Interlagos, 25 November 2012, final round (20 of 20)
2012.note: Vettel became the youngest triple champion at a chaotic, wet Interlagos finale on 25 November 2012 that he nearly lost at Turn 4 of the opening lap, where contact with Bruno Senna spun him to the back of the field with a damaged sidepod. He climbed back to sixth, which beat Fernando Alonso, second in the race, by three points, 281 to 278. It capped a season that had opened with seven different winners in the first seven races.

2011.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Suzuka, 9 October 2011, four rounds to spare (round 15 of 19)
2011.note: Needing a single point at Suzuka on 9 October 2011, Vettel finished third behind Jenson Button and Fernando Alonso and became, at 24, the youngest double world champion in the sport's history, with four races to spare. The defence was built on Saturdays as much as Sundays: 11 wins and a record 15 pole positions from 19 races, and a 122-point gap to runner-up Button by season's end.

2010.clinched: Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, 14 November 2010, final round (19 of 19)
2010.note: Vettel arrived at the Abu Dhabi finale on 14 November 2010 third in the standings, behind Alonso and Webber, in the first four-way title decider F1 had ever staged. He won from pole while Ferrari marked the wrong Red Bull, leaving Alonso and Webber stuck in midfield traffic behind Vitaly Petrov, and at 23 became the youngest world champion in the sport's history. The only time Vettel led the 2010 championship was after the chequered flag of its last race; the final margin over Alonso was four points, 256 to 252.

2009.clinched: Brazilian Grand Prix, Interlagos, 18 October 2009, one round to spare (round 16 of 17)
2009.note: Button clinched the title at Interlagos on 18 October 2009, storming from 14th on the grid to fifth with one round to spare while polesitter and closest pursuer Rubens Barrichello fell to eighth with a puncture. It completed the Brawn GP fairy tale: the team won both world championships in its only season of existence, the first constructors' crown ever taken by a debutant, with Button converting six wins from the first seven races into a 95-point total that held off Sebastian Vettel by 11.

2008.clinched: Brazilian Grand Prix, Interlagos, 2 November 2008, final round (18 of 18)
2008.note: Hamilton won his first title at Interlagos on 2 November 2008 by taking fifth place from Timo Glock at Juncao, the last corner of the last lap of the season, moments after a late shower had caught Glock out on dry tyres. Felipe Massa had won the race and was champion for around 20 seconds before the positions settled. The single-point margin, 98 to 97, made Hamilton, then 23, the youngest world champion yet, and the first British champion since Damon Hill in 1996.

2007.clinched: Brazilian Grand Prix, Interlagos, 21 October 2007, final round (17 of 17)
2007.note: Räikkönen began the final day of 2007 third in the championship, seven points behind Lewis Hamilton, and ended it champion by one, 110 to the 109 of both Hamilton and Fernando Alonso. Ferrari's pit sequencing at Interlagos on 21 October moved him ahead of teammate Felipe Massa for the win he had to have, while a gearbox glitch dropped Hamilton to seventh. It was the first time since 1986 that three drivers had taken a title fight into the season's last race.

2006.clinched: Brazilian Grand Prix, Interlagos, 22 October 2006, final round (18 of 18)
2006.note: Alonso completed back-to-back championships with second place behind Felipe Massa at Interlagos on 22 October 2006, the final round of an 18-race duel with Michael Schumacher. The contest had swung two weeks earlier at Suzuka, where Schumacher's engine let go while he led; needing only a point in Brazil, Alonso banked eight and won by 13, 134 to 121. The race doubled as Schumacher's farewell before his first retirement, and he signed off by climbing from a puncture back to fourth.

2005.clinched: Brazilian Grand Prix, Interlagos, 25 September 2005, two rounds to spare (round 17 of 19)
2005.note: Third place behind the McLarens of Juan Pablo Montoya and Kimi Räikkönen at Interlagos on 25 September 2005 made Alonso champion with two rounds to spare, and at 24 years and 59 days the youngest in the sport's history to that point. It ended Michael Schumacher's five-year reign and made him Spain's first Formula 1 world champion. Räikkönen also won seven races that year yet finished 21 points back, 133 to 112.

2004.clinched: Belgian Grand Prix, Spa-Francorchamps, 29 August 2004, four rounds to spare (round 14 of 18)
2004.note: Schumacher's seventh and final championship was sealed with second place behind Kimi Räikkönen at Spa on 29 August 2004, four rounds from the end, at the circuit where he had made his debut in 1991. He had won 12 of the season's first 13 races, missing only Monaco, and finished with 13 victories, a record at the time. Teammate Rubens Barrichello was the only driver still mathematically alive arriving in Belgium, and ended the year 34 points adrift, 148 to 114.

2003.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Suzuka, 12 October 2003, final round (16 of 16)
2003.note: Schumacher broke Fangio's 46-year-old record of five championships in the least Schumacher-like way imaginable: eighth place at the Suzuka finale on 12 October 2003, scraping the single point he needed after qualifying 14th in the wet and losing his front wing against Takuma Sato's BAR. Räikkönen, who needed to win with Schumacher scoreless, finished second to Rubens Barrichello and fell two points short, 93 to 91. No season in Ferrari's five-title run with Schumacher came closer to slipping away.

2002.clinched: French Grand Prix, Magny-Cours, 21 July 2002, six rounds to spare (round 11 of 17)
2002.note: No champion has ever finished the job earlier: Schumacher won at Magny-Cours on 21 July 2002, round 11 of 17, to claim the title in July with six races to spare, a record that still stands. The win came when Kimi Räikkönen slid on Allan McNish's oil with five laps left. Schumacher stood on the podium after every one of the season's 17 races, a feat no other driver has managed, winning 11 of them and finishing 67 points clear of teammate Rubens Barrichello.

2001.clinched: Hungarian Grand Prix, Hungaroring, 19 August 2001, four rounds to spare (round 13 of 17)
2001.note: Schumacher took his fourth championship by winning the Hungarian Grand Prix on 19 August 2001 from lights to flag, a victory that also equalled Alain Prost's all-time record of 51 wins on the same afternoon. The Ferrari one-two with Rubens Barrichello sealed the constructors' title as well, four rounds early, and made Schumacher the first back-to-back Ferrari champion since Alberto Ascari in 1953. His eventual margin over David Coulthard was 58 points, 123 to 65.

2000.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Suzuka, 8 October 2000, one round to spare (round 16 of 17)
2000.note: Schumacher ended Ferrari's 21-year wait for a drivers' champion, the first since Jody Scheckter in 1979, by beating Mika Häkkinen at Suzuka on 8 October 2000 with one round to spare. The pair traded the lead through the pit cycles until Schumacher stayed out three laps longer at the second stops, emerged in front, and controlled the run home. His third title, and first in red, closed at 108 points to Häkkinen's 89, with nine wins.

1999.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Suzuka, 31 October 1999, final round (16 of 16)
1999.note: Häkkinen settled the strangest title race of the era by winning the Suzuka finale outright on 31 October 1999, leading 50 of 53 laps after arriving four points behind Ferrari's Eddie Irvine; the final count was 76 to 74. His real rival had been missing for half the season: Michael Schumacher broke his leg in a brake-failure crash at Silverstone in July, leaving Irvine to carry Ferrari's challenge. Häkkinen went back-to-back even as Ferrari took the constructors' crown, their first since 1983.

1998.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Suzuka, 1 November 1998, final round (16 of 16)
1998.note: The 1998 decider at Suzuka on 1 November fell apart for Michael Schumacher before it began: he stalled from pole position at the second formation start and had to set off from the back of the grid, four points behind Häkkinen. He had charged back into podium contention when track debris left a slow puncture, and the tyre blew on lap 31 to end his race. Häkkinen led every lap for his eighth win of the season, sealing his first championship 100 points to 86 alongside McLaren's first constructors' title since 1991.

1997.clinched: European Grand Prix, Jerez, 26 October 1997, final round (17 of 17)
1997.note: Villeneuve took the 1997 title at the Jerez finale on 26 October, a weekend that began with the top three qualifiers setting an identical 1:21.072 and turned on lap 48, when championship leader Michael Schumacher steered into Villeneuve's Williams at the Dry Sack corner and bounced into the gravel himself. Villeneuve nursed his damaged car home in third place, enough for the crown in only his second season. In November the FIA excluded Schumacher from the championship classification altogether, which is why the records list Heinz-Harald Frentzen, 39 points back, as runner-up to Villeneuve's 81.

1996.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Suzuka, 13 October 1996, final round (16 of 16)
1996.note: Hill settled the all-Williams title fight by leading every one of the 52 laps at the Suzuka finale on 13 October 1996, his eighth win of the year, while teammate Jacques Villeneuve, nine points behind on arrival, lost a rear wheel on lap 37 and retired. Victory made him the first son of a world champion to take the title himself, 28 years after Graham Hill's second crown. It was also his last drive for Williams, and Hill called the win his leaving present to the team.
